passage: I sat in on the video call between Dhruv, in Mumbai, and Manoj, a colleague in Helsinki. Dhruv had joined the team last month and was still working out how he looked on screen. He kept his gaze slightly lowered while Manoj spoke, as he'd been taught to do out of respect for senior people. Manoj, on the other hand, held steady eye contact through the camera. After the call Manoj told me quietly he wasn't sure if Dhruv was interested. Dhruv told me later that Manoj's steady gaze felt intense, almost like a challenge. I can't say whether either of them was right. When they talked about it the next week, both laughed and agreed to explain their habits.

qa.q: In which city was Manoj?
qa.a: Manoj was in Helsinki.

qa.q: What did Manoj think of Dhruv's lowered gaze, and how did Dhruv feel about Manoj's steady one?
qa.a: Manoj wondered if Dhruv was interested, while Dhruv found Manoj's steady gaze intense, almost like a challenge.

qa.q: What could Dhruv and Manoj do to work better across their differences?
qa.a: They could explain their habits to each other, stay curious and not assume the other's gaze shows disinterest or challenge.

qa.q: How might the observer see the two men's gaze?
qa.a: The observer can't say who was right and only sees two different norms meeting, so neither is wrong.

grounding: An observer sees gaze norms differ between Dhruv and Manoj across countries and be talked through.

passage:
Week one. Avni joined the multinational team and noticed that her Swedish colleague Jomon held long, steady eye contact in meetings. At first it made her uncomfortable, since at home she looked away from seniors. She wondered if he was challenging her.

Week three. Avni learned from a team lead that in Jomon's culture direct gaze meant paying attention. She tried it herself in a one-to-one and found it awkward but not hostile.

Week five. Avni told Jomon, "I look down out of respect where I'm from." Jomon laughed. "I thought you were bored!" They agreed to say aloud what they meant. Avni felt lighter, and for the first time, she looked at him and smiled.

qa.q: Which country was Jomon's colleague from, according to Avni's notes?
qa.a: Avni's colleague Jomon is described as Swedish.

qa.q: What did Avni feel about Jomon's steady gaze at first, and how did it change?
qa.a: At first it made her uncomfortable and she wondered if he was challenging her, then she came to see it as attention and felt lighter after they talked.

qa.q: What could Avni and Jomon do to keep the misunderstanding from returning?
qa.a: They could say aloud what they mean and stay curious about each other's habits instead of stereotyping.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Avni looked down?
qa.a: He thought she was bored, so he may have felt puzzled or a little rejected.

grounding: Avni and Jomon meet different gaze norms over several weeks and adapt while staying curious.

passage: Lavanya beti, you're joining the team with the Helsinki office, so let your Dilnaz aunty tell you what I learnt. At twenty-four, I worked on a project with engineers from Finland and Brazil. On my first video meeting, the Brazilian lead, Marcos, looked straight at the camera the whole time. I found it intense, almost challenging, and kept looking down, as I did at home with seniors. Later my Finnish colleague Aino told me Marcos had asked if I was unhappy with the plan, because I never looked at him. I was shocked. I'd meant it as respect! Aino herself looked away often while thinking, and Marcos had thought she was bored too. We all laughed about it later. So we made a small rule: if you're unsure, ask. I learnt to meet Marcos's eyes more, and he learnt to give Aino her thinking pauses. Don't decide who someone is from their eyes, beti.

qa.q: Who told young Dilnaz that Marcos had asked about her?
qa.a: Her Finnish colleague Aino.

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel when she heard Marcos thought she was unhappy?
qa.a: She was shocked, since she had looked down as a sign of respect, not unhappiness.

qa.q: What choice did the team make that helped?
qa.a: They agreed to ask when unsure, and each adapted: Dilnaz met Marcos's eyes more and Marcos allowed Aino her thinking pauses.

qa.q: How did Marcos read Dilnaz's lowered gaze?
qa.a: As possible unhappiness with the plan, because she never looked at him.

grounding: Shows a young professional learning that gaze norms differ in a cross-cultural team and that adapting and asking avoids stereotypes.

passage: The video call with the Munich team kept freezing, and the product demo was due in thirty minutes. Ganga, twenty-five, was leading. Her colleague Deepak kept his eyes lowered whenever Stefan, the German manager, spoke to him directly. Stefan's voice got sharper. "Deepak, are you with us? You don't seem engaged." Deepak looked startled. Ganga knew Deepak's family had taught him that looking down while a senior speaks shows respect; he'd told her once. But on a frozen, pixelated screen, it just looked like he wasn't there. She unmuted. "Stefan, Deepak is very engaged; he wrote most of this code. I think with this bad connection, eye contact is hard to read. Deepak, could you walk us through the login fix?" Deepak looked into the camera and explained it clearly. Stefan nodded. "Very good. Thank you." After the call, Deepak said, "I'll try looking up more on video."

qa.q: How long was it until the product demo?
qa.a: Thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when Stefan asked if he was with them?
qa.a: He looked startled and was probably embarrassed, since he meant his lowered eyes as respect.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that bridged the misunderstanding?
qa.a: She explained Deepak's engagement and the hard-to-read connection, then invited him to present so his work showed.

qa.q: How did Stefan read Deepak's lowered eyes?
qa.a: As a sign Deepak wasn't engaged, not knowing it was meant as respect.

grounding: Shows a young professional bridging different gaze norms in a cross-cultural team call, adapting without stereotyping.

passage: In the Bengaluru software office, Sonali, twenty-six, noticed that her new teammate Dolma never looked the manager, Mr Pieter, in the eye during stand-ups. Pieter, who had moved from Amsterdam, liked people to hold his gaze. After a week, he said to Sonali, "Is Dolma unhappy here? She won't look at me." Sonali didn't want to guess or explain for Dolma. At lunch she asked Dolma, casually, "How are you finding Pieter?" Dolma smiled. "He's nice. But he stares so much! In my family, looking straight at a senior feels rude. I look down to be polite." Sonali laughed. "He thinks you're unhappy." Dolma's eyes widened. "Oh no." Sonali suggested she tell Pieter herself. The next day Dolma did, and Pieter laughed too. "I'll stop staring so hard. And you look up now and then?" "Deal," Dolma said. Both adjusted a little.

qa.q: Where had Mr Pieter moved from?
qa.a: From Amsterdam.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she learned Pieter thought she was unhappy?
qa.a: She was surprised and a little dismayed, her eyes widening, since she had meant to be polite.

qa.q: What did Sonali do that avoided a stereotype?
qa.a: Sonali asked Dolma directly instead of guessing or explaining for her, and suggested Dolma tell Pieter herself.

qa.q: How did Pieter respond once Dolma explained?
qa.a: He laughed, agreed to stop staring so hard, and asked her to look up now and then.

grounding: Shows young professionals learning that gaze norms differ and adapting with curiosity rather than assumptions.

passage:
"Vinita, quick question. On the call with the partner team today I kept steady eye contact the whole time, like we were trained. Their lead kept looking down at her notes whenever I spoke."
"And you decided she was bored?"
"Bored, or annoyed. Then she wrote afterwards, 'Thank you for your intense attention.' Intense? Is that nice or not?"
Vinita laughed. "Could be both. When I worked with the Lisbon office, long eye contact felt normal. On another team, a senior told me my stare felt like a challenge."
"So it depends on the country?"
"Partly. Partly on the person. Her looking down might be respect, or thinking, or just her notes."
"So what do I do?"
"Watch how they look at each other. Soften a little, glance away sometimes. And ask her how meetings usually run on their side."
Vikas opened a new message. "Asking now."

qa.q: What did the partner lead write after the call?
qa.a: She wrote, 'Thank you for your intense attention.'

qa.q: Why was Vikas unsure after reading the message?
qa.a: Vikas felt confused and a bit anxious, because 'intense' could be praise or a hint that the steady eye contact had felt like a challenge.

qa.q: What would you advise Vikas before the next call?
qa.a: Watch how the partner team looks at each other, soften the gaze a little, and ask the lead how their meetings usually run instead of assuming.

qa.q: How might the partner lead have experienced the steady eye contact?
qa.a: The lead may have felt watched or pressed, or may simply have found it keen; her looking down could have been her own way of showing respect, so each side may have misread the other.

grounding: Gaze norms differ between teams and places, so a young professional adapts and asks rather than stereotyping.
